references.text: The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 22:17-21|Matthew 22:17-21], where the Pharisees and Herodians ask Jesus the same question about whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, and Jesus answers by asking them to show him a tax coin.

The parallel passage in [ref:Mark 12:14-17|Mark 12:14-17], where Jesus is confronted with the same question about paying taxes to Caesar and gives his famous answer: "Give to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God."

In [ref:Rom 13:6-7|Romans 13:6-7], Paul teaches that Christians should pay taxes and customs to the authorities, and give honor and respect to those to whom it is due – a continuation of Jesus' principle of giving Caesar what belongs to Caesar.

[ref:5 Mos 17:15|Deuteronomy 17:15] states that Israel must not set a foreign man who is not a brother as king over them. The question about paying taxes to Caesar touches on this principle, since the Romans were a foreign occupying power.
In [ref:Luk 23:2|Luke 23:2], they accuse Jesus before the Sanhedrin and Pilate with the claim that he forbids paying taxes to Caesar – a distortion of his answer in this text.

In [ref:Matt 17:25-27|Matthew 17:25-27], Jesus discusses the temple tax with Peter, showing that although the king's children are actually free, they still pay so as not to cause offense – a principle that sheds light on Jesus' attitude toward taxes.
